Forestry Act "forest experiment" is defined as meaning the study of silviculture, forest pathology, forest entomology, forest fire protection and many other technical branches. I am sure there is no question in anyone's mind that where these technical subjects are concerned we must have trained men who are able to look after these matters.
Ia this morning's Gazette I was quite interested to read a Canadian press dispatch from British Columbia headed "More Forestry Students Said Pressing Need". The article points out that while there are 6,300 students at the University of British Columbia only 125 are registered in the faculty of forestry. The article then refers to Dr. Allen, dean of the faculty of forestry of the University of British Columbia, and has this to say:
Dr. Allen said it is conservatively estimated that in 20 years British Columbia will need 2,750 graduate foresters, 2,200 more than there are today.
If that number will be needed in British Columbia alone we get some idea of the great need throughout the whole of Canada for men technically trained in forestry. In our own province of New Brunswick we have had a school of forestry at the University of New Brunswick for over 50 years. Our graduates have gone not only to all the provinces of Canada but to the United States and, in fact, all over the world. Today we are receiving students from every province in Canada, the United States, Australia, Europe, and especially from Great Britain. They are coming to the university to take the forestry course there.
We often hear it said in the house that scholarships should be given at different universities. I do not think there is a greater need for scholarships in any branch of study today, and I would recommend to the consideration of the federal government the provision of forestry scholarships in our different universities. There are three universities which teach forestry, British Columbia, Toronto and New Brunswick. I cannot think of anything that would be better for the conservation of our forests than to have more of these men to assist in that work.
It is not my intention to take any more time this afternoon. I should like to speak about the effect that the lack of conservation of our forests has had on some of our fisheries, but I will have an opportunity to do so later on. I would simply say that the fact that the forests have been cut down along the banks of many of our streams in New Brunswick, the maritime provinces generally, Gaspe and even in Newfoundland has meant that streams, up which the Atlantic salmon go to spawn, are more or less drying up with a resulting decrease in the catch of salmon.

Conservation
Only last year the catch decreased by over 50 per cent. Men who have studied the problem contend that one of the reasons is the fact that these streams are drying up and that the spawning grounds of the salmon have been taken away from them. These are all matters which deserve careful consideration. I agree entirely with those who have this afternoon contended that this is a matter in which the dominion government is vitally interested. I am strongly in favour of the resolution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been listening with a great deal of interest to the comments made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) upon introducing his resolution. We are certainly grateful to him for providing us with an opportunity to discuss a problem of such significance.
As the hon. member pointed out, this motion is twofold. It involves, first of all, the establishment of a nation-wide conservation policy, and ensures its implementation through a federal-provincial conference. We all realize how important it is for us to make wise use of those natural resources which are the very foundation of our national economy.
Agriculture is based on use of the land, and our industries utilize electric power which could hardly exist without this use of the land. The Canadian government has long understood the importance of this problem and, in this connection, has implemented various steps in those territories over which it has direct jurisdiction.
Besides, the federal government has had legislation passed to favour all conservation projects that provinces could put into effect, such as, for instance, the Canada Forestry Act, the International River Improvements Act, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, all of which, to mention only those few, were adopted at the request of government departments to promote conservation of our natural resources.
Moreover, throughout the country, various agencies not connected with our governments, either federal or provincial, also carry out surveys and publicity projects to promote and help soil conservation.
I could not let this opportunity pass without Mentioning the enormous and very important part played in this field in the province of Quebec by the Quebec Forestry Association and our numerous 4-H clubs.
We all realize, as members who spoke before me indicated, the importance of the

conservation of our soil, of our water resources, in brief, of all our natural resources.
The motion that has been submitted to us, Mr. Speaker, would entrust this responsibility to the central authority, calling as it does for a national conservation policy. Any legislation that might come out of this motion, if it is passed, would make the central authority the primary warden of our natural resources, with ten foremen in charge of the administration of those resources under the jurisdiction of the federal government. After all, in order to be efficient, the principle of a nation-wide policy implies a central power or administration, and at the same time implies some measure of control.
The motion submitted by the hon. member is perhaps not comprehensive to that extent and has no other purpose than to interest the provinces in the establishment of a national program of conservation under which they might benefit from subsidies while remaining free to act as they would wish. In either case, I can see reasons of a constitutional, social and economic nature, which would prompt me to vote against the resolution.
Everybody here knows that, under the constitution, or rather under the British North America Act, sections 109 and 92-or more precisely under subsection 5 of section 92, not only do provinces have exclusive jurisdiction over the administration of our natural resources, but they are exclusive owners of these resources.
Federal government participation, as recommended in the motion of the hon. member, is a direct encroachment upon provincial autonomy, in a field which we have always regarded as a strictly provincial prerogative. Jurisdiction over these matters is restricted to provincial authorities, and I submit that under present conditions it is of paramount importance for the federal parliament to reject any attempt at infiltration into this sector of Canadian economy.
Canada's present expansion, and the technical advances of modern science, coupled with an influx of capital investment warranted and encouraged by the prospects of the country, have largely contributed, over the past decades, to the development of our resources from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
The increasing pace of the development of those resources has meant huge revenues to some provinces, revenues so huge, we might say, that they rank among the main items in provincial finances. We all know that the last federal-provincial conference again emphasized the pressing need for provincial governments to find alternative sources of

revenue to meet the requirement's arising from their various responsibilities.
It is therefore imperative that the provincial government retain its authority in the field of conservation and development of its resources, so that it may enjoy the necessary discretion to supervise the utilization of its soil, forests, water resources and lands.
Only thus will the provinces fully benefit from the revenues arising out of the proper development of natural resources in a country as prosperous as Canada. We have already seen that some provinces, which were hindered a few years ago in the discharge of their responsibilities by the lack of sufficient revenues, have greatly improved their financial position as a result of the development of their natural resources.
Nobody will deny the financial advantages which Alberta has derived from the development of her natural resources. I also believe that the improvement in the financial situation of British Columbia-whose per capita revenue is now greater than that of the province of Quebec, with a larger population and a larger territory-is the result of the development of her natural resources.
In short, a national conservation policy could seriously hinder the collection of revenues which provinces can derive from the development of their own natural resources.
In addition, a national policy in the field of conservation implies a measure of uniformity that would hardly be consistent with the differences in climate and topography existing from the Pacific to the Atlantic.
True, a national conservation policy could perhaps be profitable from the economic standpoint, but I maintain that we must take into account other factors besides the economy because quite often in various parts of the country the conservation of our soil, the development of our forests and water resources are definitely linked with certain political or social principles, which differ in the various provinces that make up this country.
The conservation of our resources must take into account certain regional characteristics. For instance, intensive colonization compels local authorities to promote forest development for reasons particular to the district where colonization is taking place. On the other hand, we know that specialized farming in certain districts requires proper
Conservation
irrigation. Besides, our forest industry must be protected by means which may differ according to the area concerned. Surely methods of pest control in the woodlots of the province of Quebec are unlike those which might be used to control tree pests in the forest lands of the west coast, because the trees themselves and atmospheric conditions are different.
In addition, the various provincial governments are in a better position to look after the development of our water resources.
It may be that a provincial government wishing to develop its resources more than another province will allow the production of water power to take place at the same time as some industrial developments in order to decentralize industry. Conservation and development of our natural resources may be either nationalized or left to private enterprise. Some provinces might also look for immediate revenues through the development of natural resources while others might be more interested in the stability and security resulting from a slow development of natural resources. Moreover, in the province of Quebec, a great part of our education is connected with the development of those same natural resources. In fact, the agricultural college of Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere and some faculties of the University of Montreal and the university of Quebec are closely connected with the utilization of our different natural resources in that province. I believe also that a national conservation policy could jeopardize the outcome of these various programs which, in my province, are closely linked with university education.
Of course this does not mean that the central government should not get more interested in the conservation of our soil, in the cultivation of our lands and in the maintenance and development of our power resources. Already the Department of Transport, by recommending the St. Lawrence seaway project to this parliament, has largely contributed to promote and further the development of resources in northern Quebec.
I wish to thank the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) for asking this parliament to vote the necessary subsidies for the construction of a railway in the lake St. John district, an improvement which no doubt will create an atmosphere definitely con-

Conservation
ducive to the conservation and the development of the tremendous forest reserves of that district.
A moment ago, the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), indicated that sometimes airports can help in the control of forest fire, disease or anything detrimental to them. There again, we must congratulate the federal Department of Transport for understanding that need.
As far as we are concerned, in the Charlevoix district which I have the honour to represent here, we are glad to express gratitude to the minister for having facilitated the building of that airport.
No doubt, the construction of a railway linking Charlevoix to the north shore will be another step which will greatly contribute to the development of the natural resources of that part of the province of Quebec.
Thus, since the federal government, through its different departments, has, within its jurisdiction, the means to further the conservation and the development of our resources, I intend to propose an amendment to the motion laid before the house by the hon. member. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier) :
That all the words after the word "advisability'' be deleted and the following substituted therefor: "of taking, in co-operation with the provinces, the necessary steps to establish a national inventory of the natural resources of the country with a view to permitting the federal government to grant the maximum assistance within its jurisdiction to the various provinces on soil, forest, land and water conservation."

am very happy this afternoon to have the opportunity of saying a few words in support of the important resolution which once again has been moved by the hon. member for Kootenay West. It is obvious to all of us that this is a very important question, and one which has had the unanimous endorsement of all those hon. members who have spoken up to the present time. It is hard to deal with all of the phases which would normally go into a comprehensive conservation program. It is my intention to deal with only one or two aspects of what such a program should take into account. I should like to deal with the soil and water factors which are of such importance in our economy.
I believe that the conservation problem has not had all the attention that ordinarily it
[Mr. Maltais.l
would have had, had we not been placed in such a favourable geographic position. But as our park areas become denuded of trees, were it not for weather conditions, the effects of freezing, which tend to make erosion less of a factor than it is in many other countries of the world, we would find ourselves in a much more difficult position. I believe we have deluded ourselves to some extent into believing that our agricultural and arable lands will go on indefinitely as a sort of fixed asset, and also that their productivity will continue unabated. Unless we introduce some comprehensive conservation program in this country we know from past experience in other places that that of course will not be so. We are told that the nation that neglects its soil will soon see that soil completely depleted, and of course with that ultimately the destruction of the nation itself. History records that the depletion of the soil has been a greater contributing factor to the downfall of a country than have been high taxation and other things of political consequence. Therefore it is important that we take into account the great need for an over-all comprehensive conservation program in Canada.
In western Canada we of course have had this question brought into focus because of our experience during the early and mid 1930's. During that time we had in that part of Canada what has commonly come to be known as the dust bowl area. It is one of the amazing phenomena of modern times, I believe, that this land has returned to its productivity. It is hard to understand after almost years of continuous soil erosion because of high winds. The land was abandoned, and the people never expected to go back again.
However, those of us who were there and saw what actually happened can appreciate the value of a conservation program similar to what was set up under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act back in 1938. At that time we saw soil erosion at its worst. The wind blew holes in level ground the size of this chamber. School children were let out of school at noon week in and week out because of the intensity of the dust. They could not see. It was almost like night. This was disastrous to our economy. Think of the years and the lives that were wasted. People had to leave the land, go into other industries, move to different parts of the country to make a new start. These are some of the things we should try to avoid if at all possible.

In spite of those disastrous times I have mentioned we in this country still have a tendency to think of our natural resources as oil wells, mineral deposits, timber lands, and so forth. Yet oil wells have a very embarrassing habit of going dry. Mines end up as empty holes in the ground. The only renewable resource, the only really important resource, is our land. After all, if it is properly cared for it will go on producing indefinitely. As a matter of fact, under proper management I think it can safely be said that its productivity increases.
This is no local problem it is a national problem. Because it has been tackled more or less on a local basis throughout different parts of the country we have a tendency to think that it is a local problem rather than a national problem. Under the British North America Act certain jurisdiction in this regard is given to the provinces. Experimental and scientific research comes under the jurisdiction of the federal government. In times of national disaster, in times such as I pointed out happened in western Canada during the dust bowl days of the 1930's, the problem was such that no province by itself could cope with it. Therefore the federal government recognized that it was beyond the capacity of a province and they came into the picture.
In 1938 there was set up in the prairie provinces the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, commonly known as P.F.R.A. To give some indication of what was accomplished under the most adverse conditions imaginable, in 1938 and 1939 it took 58 acres of land to pasture one head of livestock in this area, which comprises some several million acres in southern Saskatchewan, and I imagine the same thing applied to southern Alberta and to other places that experienced similar conditions. After the act came into force it was a matter of only a short period of time until three head of cattle could be grazed successfully on the same 58 acres of land. That again is a clear indication of the great value of the practical application of scientific know-how to land and soil management.
We have now some 53 of these community pastures, as they are called, comprising several thousand acres, but the amazing thing is that in Saskatchewan there are some 23 million acres of land considered to be unfit for agricultural purposes. This is located in what is known as the brown soil zone. The P.F.A.A. people have carried out wide investigations and surveys of this area and have come up with statistics to prove that farmers cannot survive on this type of soil. Yet of those 23 million acres in Saskatchewan, 15 million acres are under cultivation. There
Conservation
is great need for conservation measures to get out of that land the production of which it is capable. In other words we are wasting some 23 million acres of land in Saskatchewan, land which could make a great contribution to the economic stability of this country.
During the depression years in Saskatchewan, brought about by the factors I mentioned a moment ago, it cost the people of Canada in the way of direct relief $184 million, to say nothing of the tremendous losses in capital investment. The P.F.R.A. made a great contribution to checking that tremendous loss. Approximately $76 million was spent under that act, money well spent.
We must remember that hunger is still the greatest problem in the world today. Considerable research has been done by FAO in this regard. We talk about overproduction, surpluses of agricultural products and so on, but I do not think anyone who has investigated the problem will say there is overproduction. Rather it is underconsumption. We need a distribution system to see that our production gets into the hands of the people who need it.
It is estimated by the food and agriculture organization that there are some 2-7 billion acres of arable land in the world. It might be interesting to note that in Canada, where we consider we have an unlimited number of acres, only 3 per cent of our land is arable. That is quite a small percentage when we consider the situation prevailing in other countries. For instance, in the United States some 24 per cent of the land body is arable; in the United Kingdom the arable land constitutes 30 per cent of the total land body, and in some of the Scandinavian countries the percentage is as high as 65.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate on the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Kootenay West I intend to confine my remarks to our forest resources in Canada. Here in my notes I have numerous figures which I may state at the beginning have been taken from the dominion bureau of statistics,
fMr. Bryson.]
from departmental reports and from the reports of the pulp and paper association of Canada.
I believe that in order to ascertain the degree of conservation that is required in Canada at this particular time as far as our forests are concerned, it is necessary first to get some idea of the extent of our forest resources, then to have some idea of the value which our forest resources have in our economy and, third, the rate at which our forest resources are being depleted and the problems of conservation they present. Then I should like to speak for a moment with regard to the procedures that are now being adopted in relation to those problems of conservation. Finally I should like to say a few words about conservation in my own province, following the same five points.
Our forests in Canada extend over a very wide area and are exceeded only by those of two other countries, namely the tropical forests of Brazil and the forests of Russia. Our forests in Canada extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific ocean, at times narrowing to a width of 600 miles and at other times widening to a width of 1,300 miles. The total forest area is approximately one and a half million square miles or 42 per cent of the total land area.
This total forest area is divided into two categories. One is called the unproductive area. This area lies along the northern fringe of vegetation and has an area of 670,000 square miles, or 45 per cent of the forested area of Canada. I sometimes disagree with this term "unproductive area." I think that is the terminology of the foresters. It may have some value in the sense that it means a portion of our forests which does not produce merchantable timber, but the unproductive area is unproductive only in that sense, because this unproductive area of our forests does give to us a large part of the habitat of our wildlife, and also gives us great controls to regulate our water flow.
Of the productive area, 830,000 square miles or 55 per cent of our forested area, it is here we find that the forest industries are getting most of their raw materials. This productive area again is subdivided into two classes, one called the accessible area, having an area of 580,000 square miles or 70 per cent of the productive area. The inaccessible area, or 30 per cent of the productive area, is an area of 250,000 square miles. This term "inaccessible" is of course nothing more than a relative term, because the areas that are today considered inaccessible may tomorrow be accessible by the building of roads or railways or the establishment of mills or the putting of new equipment on the market.

Of our trees in Canada today, there are roughly 177 different types. Of these, 55 have commercial value, and of these 55 we have 23 softwoods and about 32 hardwoods.
Having had a look at the extent of our forest resources in Canada, I should like for a moment to spend some time on the value of the forest resource in our economy. If we took productive area alone, 830,000 square miles, and worked this out, we would find that this would be equivalent to 180 acres of productive forest land for each family of five. Based on forestry estimates, 180 acres would produce in perpetuity about 60 cords of wood annually, which at present prices would be equivalent to $1,500 per year. If we were to take the importance of the pulp and paper industry in our economy, which uses about one quarter of the actual consumption of wood, we would realize that of the money which Canadians earn, one dollar out of every eight is earned by those engaged in the pulp and paper industry. In the approximately 80 companies now operating 130 mills in seven provinces in Canada, over 300,000 men are employed directly while many more thousands are employed indirectly.
Without this great product Canada would not be the international trader that she is. The value of the pulp and paper industry to Canada exceeds the value of wheat and all grains. It is equal to the total national output of all minerals. Every hour of the day here in Canada 1,000 tons of paper and pulp is being made by our mills, having a value of approximately $140,000, or a total of $1-1 billion a year. Twenty per cent of all exports are made up of paper and pulp products, and of our exports to the United States one-third are from the paper and pulp industry.
We might have a look for a moment at the value of our forests with regard to personal holdings. It has been said that 7 per cent of the forested area in Canada is privately owned. I agree that this, of course, is correct. The area of privately owned land is 97,000 square miles, but I would suggest that, although this statement is true, it does not give a true picture of the actual holdings, for the simple reason that the land that is now privately owned is situated in that part of Canada where the most prolific growth can be obtained. I would suggest therefore that the number of square miles of land privately owned should not be calculated with reference to the total forested area but should be calculated with reference to the productive area.
If we were to do that, we would find that the privately owned land represents 12 tier 67509-101
Conservation
cent of the total productive area. On the other hand, these privately owned lands are among the most accessible forest lands in Canada, and I would therefore go on and say that not only should the private lands of Canada be calculated with reference to the productive area but also with reference to the accessible productive area. We would then find that the privately owned lands would form 17 per cent of the accessible productive area.
In different provinces various percentages of forest land are privately owned. In Prince Edward Island, for example, nearly all the forest land is privately owned. In Nova Scotia 73 per cent of the forest land is privately owned, half of which consists of areas over 1,000 acres. In New Brunswick the percentage is 50 per cent; in Newfoundland 16 per cent; in Quebec 6 per cent; in Ontario 8 per cent; in Manitoba 7 per cent; in Saskatchewan 7 per cent; in Alberta 7 per cent; and in British Columbia 4 per cent. May I say that these percentages refer to total forested areas.
I should like now to have a look for a moment at the rate at which it is calculated that our forests are being depleted. For the ten years 1941 to 1950 the average utilization was 2 [DOT] 843 billion cubic feet. For the ten years 1942 to 1951 there was a slight increase, the average annual utilization for that period being 2 [DOT] 935 billion cubic feet. The utilization for the year 1952 alone was 3-545 billion cubic feet.
It will be noticed here that in the year 1952 there was a very definite increase. In talking about depletion we must not only, of course, refer to utilization. It is also necessary to refer to wastage. In the years I have mentioned wastage due to fire, insects and disease amounted to an annual average, for the ten years 1941 to 1950, of 732 million cubic feet, for the ten years 1942 to 1951 an average of 675 million cubic feet, and for the year 1952, 790 million cubic feet. If these figures are related to the total product which the forest is able to supply we find that over the ten years 1942 to 1951, the annual depletion was at the rate of 1 * 3 per cent of the accessible area or 0-9 per cent of the productive area or 2-9 per cent of the occupied area. For the year 1952 the depletion for the total productive area was 1 [DOT] 1 per cent, for the occupied area 3 [DOT] 5 per cent and for the accessible area 1 [DOT] 6 per cent.
If we take these figures and analyse them some very interesting facts can be found. First, we note that the rate of depletion is increasing. Second, we note that the annual rate of depletion in the occupied area wa*

Conservation
3-5 per cent for the year 1952. No forest could ever hope to maintain a sustained annual yield with a 3-5 per cent depletion in any one year or over a period of years. But we must remember that this 3 * 5 per cent refers only to the occupied area, and the occupied area is of course considerably less than the total forested area of Canada. The total occupied area is actually 38 per cent of the productive area. If this is written in terms of the productive area, 1 [DOT] 1 per cent, we can easily see that with a rotation program of 70 years a depletion of 1-1 per cent can- easily be maintained. While it may be true that in the accessible and occupied areas the percentage of depletion has been rather high, I suggest that when we talk about the rate of depletion it should be referred to the total productive area.
But another lesson comes from this, Mr. Speaker. It means that in the areas that are being logged today excessive cutting in all probability is taking place. But if the rate is referred to the whole area then the rate of cutting is not excessive, which points out the need for a very strong forest management program in Canada so that rather than cutting timber stands that are not old enough to be cut, there will be direction toward the cutting of timber in those stands that are mature and overstocked.
I believe these figures indicate the directions in which conservation measures are most likely to be successful, and I would suggest that there are five. First of all, there should be a program of sound forest management. Second, there should be direction toward the cutting of timber on mature stands that are overstocked. Third, there should be good cutting practice with controlled reforestation, seeding and planting programs not only to renew the forests that have been cut but also to augment them, for I believe that in any forest area that has been cut it is not only possible to produce a forest equally as good as the one that was cut, but that under proper management it is possible to produce a forest that is better. In other words, we not only have renewal but we also have augmentation. Fourth, we need an effective fire prevention program. Of course many of our provinces today do have fire prevention programs that are effective. Fifth, we need adequate scientific research to discover and control attacks by insect and disease.
If these five points are to be the points of a conservation program, let us look for a moment and see how these five points are being carried out by provincial governments, assisted by the federal government and assisted by private enterprise. In 1949 this

parliament passed the Canada Forestry Act. Two years later, in May, 1951, there was a federal-provincial conference with reference to conservation. Following the passing of the Canada Forestry Act there was an agreement with some of the provinces whereby the federal government agreed to pay one-half the cost of forest inventories. They agreed to pay $10 per thousand for planted trees, $1 per acre for seeding and one-fifth of the cost of operation of tree nurseries.
Up to March 31, 1954, under this program ground surveys had been done on 200,000 square miles of Canada's forest lands, air surveys had been done on 500,000 square miles, and inventory reports had been received on over 400,000 square miles. Up to March 31, 1955, planting had exceeded 50 million trees over an estimated area of 60,000 acres, and seeding had been done over 6,000 acres. It is estimated that by the end of March, 1956, nearly $5 million will have been spent by the federal government on this program initiated under the Canada Forestry Act of 1949.
Added to this we have the research facilities of the federal government. We have the prevention measures by provincial governments and also by private enterprise. I believe that by provincial governments and by private enterprise a very excellent job is being done in this respect. We also have expenditures by the lumbering industry and expenditure on research and control by the Canadian pulp and paper association which exceeds the expenditure of all provincial governments combined.
I believe that a fairly good program of conservation is now in effect. It remains to be seen how effective it will be over the next few years and how well the program as outlined can be implemented. But I believe we can go forward with the hope that Canada's forests will continue to produce sufficient wood for our lumbering industry and for the pulp and paper industry. Mr. Gordon Godwin, woodlands manager for the Ontario division of the Ontario Paper Company Limited, last year said this, as found on page 2 of his printed speech, when speaking to the Rotary club of Woodstock, Ontario:
Thus with all inventory withdrawals accounted for, and in consideration of growth rates, it is clear that we are in no danger of exhausting our forests.
Also, Mr. Speaker, in the annual report of the president of the Canadian pulp and paper association for the year 1955, at page 8 the president states:
The pulpwood harvested last year for the industry increased by about 10 per cent and exceeded 13 million cords. About one-third of this wood was purchased and two-thirds came from company

limits. The limit cut. represented a harvest of less than 8 cubic feet per acre averaged over all the woodlands of the industry. These woodlands can most certainly support such a cut in perpetuity and, under present management methods, can support an increasing cut in the years to come.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to forestry resources conservation measures within my own province of Newfoundland. I do not believe there is any province across the whole country of Canada that is more conservation conscious than is Newfoundland. I believe we may have the earliest conservation measures in existence across this land, going back into the early history of Newfoundland, to the year 1610 when a Bristol merchant by the name of John Guy came to Newfoundland and established a settlement at Cupids. There in 1610 he made this ruling: "No person shall set fire in the woods". It may be that this regulation made early in 1610 was the first conservation measure on the North American continent.
I might add that it was at this time, under the administration of John Guy, that the first forest survey in Newfoundland was made. I agree, of course, that it applied only to that area of Newfoundland over which John Guy had the authority of administration. But 150 years later Sir Hugh Palliser, a governor of Newfoundland, speaking of Labrador, said that any person setting fire in the woods should be brought to St. John's, the capital of the province, and there tried before him. That was in the year 1767.
From that time onward not a great deal was done with the forestry resources in Newfoundland, but in 1919 a branch of the department of agriculture and mines was set up for the purpose of looking after our forest resources. In 1953 a new policy for forest management was brought into effect. At the present time the total forest lands of Newfoundland-and I am referring only to the island-are divided into 250 operational zones. In some of these zones studies have been carried out with relation to cutting rules and allowable cuts. In those management zones more concentrated studies have been carried out with the idea of getting facts and figures relating to the amount of wood which could be cut, the allowable cut and plans for a more effective management program. Of course the earlier settlers who came to Newfoundland came there to fish, but they were not there very long before they were able to see clearly the relation between the fishing and the forest industries.
There was a gradual development of the lumbering industry. For example, some of the old water wheels are still there. But it was not until 1890 that Newfoundland entered the export lumber business. It was
Conservation
not until 1897 that the first pulp mill was established in Newfoundland. This pulp mill operated, I believe, for a period of five years. Then in 1909 the Anglo-Newfoundland Development Company started that great mill at Grand Falls. In 1925 the Newfoundland Power and Paper Company began the great newsprint mill on the Humber river. This mill was later transferred to the International Power and Paper Company in 1926 and, in 1938, to the great Bowater organization.
The importance of forest industries to the economy of Newfoundland may well be shown by this statement, and I am reading from the estimated income of Newfoundland for the year 1955. The estimated income from all forest industries is rated at $64 million, or 31-6 per cent of the total income. The income next to that of forest industries was that of mining but it was much less, being only 12-3 per cent. The fishing industry was far less, bringing in only $20 million or 9-8 per cent of the total annual income.
In 1954 the provincial government of Newfoundland authorized a royal commission to be established to look into the problems of conservation in Newfoundland, along with, of course, many other forestry problems. I have here a copy of this report. As far as I can see, Mr. Speaker, the essence of this report is the same as what I have given for the forests of Canada as a whole, namely that in some areas there is considerable overcutting but that for the forests in general there is plenty of forest land to allow the present industries to carry on for some considerable time.
This does not, however, take into account the forest resources in Labrador. No complete forest inventory has been made of the forest resources of Newfoundland Labrador; but from what aerial surveys have been made, as well as from ground surveys, it is estimated that the major part of the forest resources of Newfoundland Labrador are concentrated at three points. These are in the lake Melville area, having a total production of 30 million cords; in the Sandwich bay area, having a total production of 11 million cords, and on the southeast coast of Labrador, having a total production of 8 million cords. These figures give a total of 49 million cords, an amount which would look after the industries of Newfoundland for some time, since they have an annual rate of depletion of a little less than 1 million cords per year.
Having due regard to these facts, the fact that there was a federal-provincial conference in 1951, the fact that in 1954 a convention was held by the Canadian forestry association, and the fact there is some indication that the forestry association will continue with its convention in 1956, I believe

Conservation
that no federal-provincial conference is necessary at this time. To the hon. member for Kootenay West I should like to say that this is a problem which needs to be watched continually if we wish to be sure that our forestry resources are not going to be depleted beyond recognized limits.
I believe that the real conservation is the conservation which is put into effect when there is no danger of having our resources depleted. I should like to commend the hon. member for Kootenay West for having brought forward this resolution, and I hope it will be brought forward again. I believe that the conservation of our natural resources is a problem that needs to be tackled at various times in this house. After all, Mr. Speaker, our natural resources do not belong to us. We are not the owners; we are only the temporary tenants. I should hope that here, in this great land of Canada, some conservation program can be carried on so that we may hand over to posterity those natural resources, improved if possible but never impaired.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member who just spoke for his excellent contribution to this discussion this afternoon. At the same time I should like to express a word of appreciation to the hon. member for Kootenay West who through his resolution has afforded us this opportunity. Obviously the subject of conservation is of tremendous interest in this house. Every year when it comes under discussion we have a wide, representative debate.
This all to the good because, as many hon. members have already indicated, the topic of conservation is of tremendous importance to Canada. We are passing into a phase of development where everyone is seriously concerned and preoccupied with the necessity of conserving our rich resources. From the standpoint of members from the prairie regions, it might appear that we are in possession of limitless land resources that could never be exhausted under any circumstances. However, already there are ominous statistics available which indicated that the time is long overdue when some positive action must be taken if we are to continue the degree of fertility we have in that section of the country.
Actually, the relationship of arable land to the total area of each of the prairie provinces is very small indeed. The Rand McNally standard world atlas, 1953 edition, indicates that in Manitoba only 6 per cent of the total land area is arable. In Saskatchewan we have 21 per cent and in Alberta 13 per cent.

There are further statistics which indicate that during the period of the thirties, in particular, and up until 1941, we abandoned some 4 million farm acres in western Canada. Between 1921 and 1940 some 267,938 acres of land in Manitoba went out of cultivation, largely due to soil erosion. Those figures serve to indicate, I feel, that this is a matter that requires urgent attention.
The point I should like to stress is the need for a nation-wide policy to cope with the problem. I shall follow the example of the hon. member for Kootenay West in using the word "nation-wide" rather than national. Without exception from all sides of the house, every time this topic is discussed, we have the unanimous opinion that conservation is important. However, when we get down to the fine point we always run afoul of the problem of federal and provincial responsibility. Last year as I recall we had an excellent discussion, but in the final analysis I think it was the Minister of Agriculture who justified continued inactivity by indicating that it would be necessary for the provincial governments to take the initiative in this matter.
There are examples where the contrary has been true. Indeed, the only real occasion when a comprehensive attempt was made to deal with the problem was in 1935, when the Conservative government of that day inaugurated the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. This was initiated by the federal government. The P.F.R.A. conservation work was placed under the jurisdiction of the federal department of agriculture. It incorporated the services of all agricultural research across the country. Soil surveys were expanded, and research was instigated at appropriate universities by plant breeders, soil scientists, agricultural engineers and agricultural economists. The extension services of the provincial departments of agriculture were helpful in taking the information arising from the various activities under P.F.R.A. to the individual farmers. The act provided for an advisory committee with representation from the provinces as well as from the federal government.
We have a precedent, therefore, for nationwide activity, at least in one important aspect of this problem. The argument that usually winds up this debate, to the effect that in order to get action we must have provincial government initiative, does not necessarily apply in view of the precedent I have just mentioned.
I am mainly interested in this problem because of the continued difficulty that we have

with flooding in Manitoba. There is a concrete example of national co-operation on this particular problem as well. Last fall a very important flood control project was commenced in my constituency on Pipestone creek. It is perhaps a relatively small development, but it does involve the expenditure of some $200,000. This Pipestone project is being jointly financed by the federal, provincial and municipal governments. Through P.F.R.A. the federal government will pay about half the cost. The provincial government will pay about one-third, and the remainder of the cost will be split between the municipalities of Pipestone and Sifton. There is also another federal department participating in this particular project. There is an Indian reserve in the area, so the federal Indian affairs department is participating in the scheme. I mention this example merely to demonstrate that it is possible to get joint action on these important measures.
If I am given two minutes, Mr. Speaker,
I think I can bring my remarks to a conclusion. I mention this subject of flooding particularly, and in doing so I do not exclude the general problem outlined in the resolution in connection with soil, forest and water conservation. I believe that flooding is directly connected to the problems that arise in regard to soil and forest preservation. I think it can be easily demonstrated that flooding, which we sometimes refer to as an act of God, can be more properly described as an act of man. I am thinking particularly of those murderous flash floods that have done such extensive damage in the various provinces during recent years. The flash flood on the Humber river, for example, could easily have arisen from the fact that forest reserves in Ontario have been allowed to diminish to a point where they are a small percentage of the total land area.
According to Mr. Bodsworth, who writes in Maclean's magazine, we have not only stripped the trees from the agricultural land but we have deforested 8,000 square miles of land so infertile that only trees will grow on it. He says:
Germany, though fighting for living space in two wars, has 27 per cent of its land in forests. Canada, at the rate it is now reforesting its overcleared agricultural areas, will not have an adequate forest cover until 2750-if runaway water has not carried all of our topsoil into the oceans long before that time.
He goes on to refer to the tremendous loss of topsoil that occurred during the Humber river flood, when University of Toronto scientists measured the silt content of one of the three branches of that river and found it was carrying 2,700 tons of soil per hour into lake Ontario. Now, I do not believe I have to
Conservation
stress further at this point, mainly because of lack of time, that we have an urgent problem on our hands which can only be successfully coped with if the terms of the resolution are carried out, and nation-wide consideration given to this matter at the earliest possible moment.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the mover of the resolution now before the house is a champion of conservation, as are all other hon. members of the house.
The conservation of our natural resources is one of the most important matters that can be debated here and I believe I am not mistaken in stating that we all agree on that point. Moreover, being conscious of our responsibilities, we all know that it is our privilege and duty as Canadian citizens to promote at all times the cause of conservation of our natural resources, in all its forms.
That is the principle which leads me to speak in the debate and I hope that my humble contribution will justify the valuable time that I must necessarily take to express my views on this subject.
Each time conservation has been mentioned in the house, whether on the occasion of government legislation-and there have been several instances in the past few years-or whether the matter has come up as a result of a motion from a private member, such as this one, the problem has always given rise to interesting and most fruitful debates.
The conservation of our natural resources interests all those who have the welfare of society and the future of the nation at heart. We all speak feelingly in the matter. It has long been the subject of debate in provincial legislatures. It has also been the main topic of several conferences and meetings across the country, and all classes of citizens have made their views known on the matter. All of us want to discharge our responsibility towards future generations, and make sure that our natural resources will not be depleted but preserved for use by our successors. We also wish that their development may increase In proportion to the population.

Conservation
Unfortunately, the natural resources of our country have not always been dealt with according to the principles of true conservation, nor have they received all the attention they deserved. In the past, we have been far too wasteful of our resources. In the early days of the colony, for instance, the abundance of trees was, for the settler, an obstacle to colonization. For the first settlers in this country, the forest was almost an enemy which had to be defeated to make land available for cultivation. It has been pushed back with the axe and even with fire; vast spaces of land which should never have been cleared were thus turned into unproductive deserts. In the years which followed the period of settlement, unscrupulous operators, joining efforts with the settlers, did not show any better judgment in their treatment of the forest. Our forest resources have not been dealt with properly.
Again today we do not always show our forests all the respect they deserve. Today, one cannot understand that the forest should still fall prey to human greed.
There are still too many people bent upon drawing from the forest the greatest immediate profits possible without regard for [DOT]consequences. We must put an end to these unforgivable abuses. It is the duty of provincial governments to show more severity and to bring to reason those unscrupulous operators.
Yet it is because of its forests that Canada is foremost among paper producers of the world. The forest is the great regulator of the streams which water our lands and supply our power plants. It protects against erosion and safeguards our wild life. Canadian forests, and the industries they supply, play a vital part in our national economy. Each year, they bring wealth to our country and contribute to the economic stability of the whole nation. At present, hundreds of thousands of people earn their living in those industries.
We are prone to consider that the forest is an inexhaustible source of wealth. It should not be forgotten however, that at this time our forest industries are running at full capacity and that there is very real danger that this system of high speed cutting may disrupt the balance of nature and that the forest may not have sufficient time to renew itself.
Our Canadian forest must not be allowed to die. Should this ever come about the whole national economy would suffer a grievous blow. Governments, industry and the public
.
generally must therefore take the necessary steps so that the forest may remain productive and protected against its enemies: man, fire, tree diseases and insects.
It has often been demonstrated that in the past governments have been lacking in vision and that industry, and the public in general, have been guilty of unforgivable abuses in the exploitation of our forests, with the result that over vast stretches of land the forest has become unable to ensure its own regrowth without human intervention and recourse to expensive artificial means.
Fortunately, over the past thirty years, the necessity of conservation has been better understood. At the present time, for instance, lumber companies are more alert. They take a greater interest in the future of our forestry resources and are active in the fields of forest management and silviculture. Reforestation has ensured sustained yields to some of our largest operators. Each year the industry spends considerable sums of money in the opening of access roads, fire prevention, research of all kinds and surveys of improved methods of operation. These are essential contributions on the part of industry. They must be continued and governments should make it their responsibility to encourage them as much as possible.
I should add at this point that the provinces, which are primarily responsible for the administration and conservation of our forests, of which they are the owners, are increasingly conscious of their duty as regards forest management and conservation. Nevertheless since they are the real owners of the greater part of the forest area under their control, we have a right to expect that they continue to encourage conservation in all its various forms and in every possible field.
I should very much like to remind the house once more, Mr. Speaker, of the magnificent work accomplished in the field of conservation by the Canadian Forestry Association, 1'Association Forestiere Quebecoise and all the various groups affiliated to the latter organization, such as the Quebec 4-H clubs and the regional forestry groups of which there are eight in all.
Over the past fifteen years these various associations have unceasingly alerted public opinion about the necessity of protecting and conserving our natural resources. If the interest of the Canadian public in forestry has been constantly increasing over the last few years, this is due to the activities of these various groups.

The Quebec Forestry Association was set up in 1939 by a group of public-spirited citizens who were determined to promote by all possible means the education of the public regarding the protection and the conservation of our natural resources, and more particularly our forests. For more than 15 years it has kept these vital problems before public opinion.
The Quebec Forestry Association does its educational work among French-speaking people in Canada, and its activities extend from one end of the country to the other. It is held in high repute not only in this country but in the United States and in other foreign countries. It is recognized as the best qualified organization to inform the public on the forest situation and it is regarded as the best medium for voicing public opinion on matters of conservation.
The aims of the association are to make French-speaking people in Canada conservation minded in order that the state may legislate more easily and more efficiently in that field. Its aims include also forest fire prevention, insect and disease control, and it conducts educational campaigns in favour of forest management, forestry and sound lumbering.
The association and its branches have a membership of more than 30,000, and their annual budget exceeds $175,000. The results recorded up to now are more than satisfactory, and we can be proud of the work done by these different organizations.
Public opinion has been aroused. The press, the radio, our public men and our clergy as well as associations, clubs and big business, all talk now of forest conservation as of something possible and necessary; it is even part of their activities. And, more important still; through the publicity thus carried out by the association, the public is beginning to realize the importance and necessity of such legislation passed by governments to regulate the utilization of natural resources such as the forests, fauna, rivers and land.
If I spoke at such length of the various activities of our forestry associations, it is because, to my mind, they deserve to be brought to the fore. With a very restricted budget, they do splendid work which must not pass unnoticed.
I should like at this point to appeal once again to the government and, to this effect, I urge upon the Minister of Northern Affairs
Conservation
and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) to recommend a more substantial assistance to the Canadian Forestry Association and to 1'Association Forestiere Quebecoise. This year, the estimates include an amount of $10,000 for that purpose and I should ask him to consider seriously the advisability of increasing that amount to $40,000 or $50,000. That would be one of the best investments the federal government could make for the cause of conservation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what should the federal government's attitude be as regards conservation of our national resources. If we consider the country as a whole and if we admit that forestry, agriculture, mining and manufacturing are the four mainstays of our economic, financial and industrial organization, we soon realize how important it is to strive for the conservation of our soil, our forests, our water resources and our mineral resources. We must consider this problem as being national, indeed international, in scope.
This government and its predecessors did not fail, in the course of the last twenty-five or thirty years, to take the necessary steps to co-operate with industry, with provincial governments and with our neighbours to the south, in order to intensify the conservation of the natural resources of our continent. And so we find on the statute books of Canada such laws as the Canada Forestry Act, the Canada Water Conservation Assistance Act, the Eastern Rocky Mountains Forest Conservation Act, the International River Improvements Act, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, to mention but these few. Each of these acts was passed for the benefit of any province wishing to avail itself of its provisions.
It might be good at this point to ask ourselves whether all provincial governments take advantage of these acts as they should, whether there is reticence or negligence on the part of some provincial governments when it is merely a matter of availing themselves of the assistance offered to them by the federal government. I wonder what practical results we could expect from a federal-provincial conference on conservation.
And there are many other fields where the federal government is doing a good job in matters of soil conservation, forestry and water resources. May I mention first the forestry research branch, which has made

conservation
and is still making advanced studies in tree culture, cutting, protection, timber reserves, reforestation, utilization, preservation, technology and chemistry.
In a general way, the federal government administers an extensive policy of conservation in the fields under its jurisdiction. Part of this program is related to studies and research works of all kinds in matters of agriculture, forestry and water resources.
On reading the last report of the forestry division of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, I found encouragement in the fact that seven provinces took advantage of the Canada Forestry Act and that, in a not too distant future, they will have completed the inventory of their forestry resources. It is also very encouraging to find that more than 48 million trees have been planted in six provinces according to the regulations passed under the same legislation.
It is most interesting to read in the same report that the federal government has made available to the province of New Brunswick an amount of $3 million for extermination of the spruce bud worm. This large scale experiment has already enabled the treatment of several thousand square miles, and apparently the work will continue next year as a substantial enough item appears in the 1955-56 estimates.
I could quote several other excerpts from the report I just mentioned, on hydraulics, for instance, hydrometry, forestry economy, the forestry research service, the forestry inventory section and the forestry product laboratory service. Each of these items, vying in interest with the others, shows how much federal legislation is promoting better use and greater conservation of our natural resources.
At this point I want to associate myself with the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) in congratulating the officers and technicians in charge of the federal forestry service. They are doing a good job and we can consider ourselves lucky to have employees of that calibre to direct the activities of this important department.
Mr. Speaker, it must be admitted that the federal government is giving valuable assistance to the provincial governments in the field of conservation. If the provinces are really willing to take every possible advantage of this assistance, there is reason to hope that we will obtain the desired results.

In spite of the progress achieved in this field, much remains to be done. It is not an easy problem, as I have already said, to go to the limit of our resources in matters of conservation. As a rule, such problems are solved through compromise and co-operation.
Here let me emphasize that the ultimate purpose of the resolution of the hon. member for Kootenay West is to establish a nationwide uniform policy on soil, forestry, water conservation and land use.
To achieve this, the hon. member suggests the calling of a federal-provincial conference.
It seems, at first, that there should be no objection to the establishment of a national conservation policy; on the contrary, it would seem to us an absolute necessity. On the other hand, in a case like this, might not certain people consider the expressions "national policy" or "national projects" as an infringement on provincial rights? Might not such words incite certain provinces to state that the central government wants to deprive them of some of their vested power? I am putting this question because past experience has shown that it was not always wise to initiate national policies in matters that were constitutionally under provincial jurisdiction.
As I said before in this house, I feel that one of the most important tasks faced by the various governments, by industry and the people in general would consist in defining responsibilities and lacks, so as to determine the logical means to solve any existing difficulty. The problem remains the same, and brings to the minds of some Canadians questions of great import that are still waiting for a clear answer.
How serious is our forest problem? What should we do in order to conserve this national asset? What ideal aim should industry and the various governments pursue? If there were any danger to lose this very important asset, what should be done to avoid such a disaster? How can we maintain each small lot of our woodlands in constant production?
I am repeating all those questions which I asked before in order to show that the problem with which we are concerned is not such that it could be solved during a federal-provincial conference. We have many reasons for not believing that such a conference would enable the country to establish a nation-wide conservation policy. The prob-

lem is too intricate and covers too large a field to leave any hope that it could be solved without preliminary study and without genuine co-operation on the part of all concerned.
This afternoon, the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais) moved an amendment which, I think, most members of the house should welcome. However, I, for one, insist again on suggesting that a special committee should be established. I feel that we, as a legislature, could do a better job by requesting that a special committee of the house be established in order to carry on further studies and inquiries on that subject which we all have at heart. It is quite possible that a thorough report on the matter might indicate the best way of considering the forestry problem, and the problem of the conservation of our resources as well.
It is obvious that the federal government wants to do everything in its power, at the present time, to encourage conservation. Furthermore, the legislation passed so far, the facilities provided to industry and to the provincial governments', and the moneys which are being voted every year for that purpose are so much evidence that this government is well prepared to really help those who want to help themselves.

I wish to deal for a few moments this evening-and this is the subject matter of my few words-with the lake shore erosion and water levels bordering on and surrounding lake Ontario. I have sometimes felt that my voice and those of one or two other members were crying in the wilderness in this
Conservation
house, because oil and on for the past 20 years this has been one subject in which I have been very much interested. On April 20, 1951, I said in this house:
In the immediate vicinity of Hamilton beach and Van Wagner's beach just a few months ago they experienced a great deal of trouble, and many houses have been practically washed away. The common answer to that is:	Well, they should not
have built so near the shore line. In many instances the older houses that were built years ago were built a considerable distance from the shore line at that time, but because of this constant erosion, in some instances up to six and often nearly seven feet a year over the past 15 or 20 years, the shore line has receded upwards of 200 feet. A serious condition is facing the people in the Niagara peninsula.

The brief is as follows:
The Canadian
Lake Ontario Property Protection Association
Whereas Her Majesty's government has approved the recommendation of the international joint commission to control the water level of lake Ontario contrary to nature, we, the property owners ask for your consideration of the following statements:
Whereas the natural water levels of lake Ontario with the addition of diverted waters, and the removal of the Gut dam, has maintained fluctuating level below 245 feet minimum, and 247 feet maximum, and
Whereas Her Majesty's government approved the diversion of waters to assist the hydro commission, and has now sanctioned a fluctuating level of 244-248 feet:
We therefore request Her Majesty's government to give serious consideration to the property owners' problems.
At various times members of parliament, realizing the need, and the responsibility of the government for assistance, have brought this problem up for discussion and have been offered partial assistance; but owing to the inability of the municipalities to meet their quota due to insufficient funds, the offer was withdrawn.
We realize, too, that mistakes can be made in such a mammoth undertaking, and one that caused millions o( dollars worth of damage to property owners, and much loss of land, was the diverting of waters into lake Ontario-which is the lowest of the great lakes-without making provisions for increased outflow. This association pressed for the removal of the Gut dam, and arranged for a tour of inspection of the international joint commission,

Conservation
thus convincing the commission of the seriousness of the situation; and the removal brought immediate relief.
In view of the fact that the findings of the select committee, formed by the provincial government to study erosion was never tabled, and also that no cabinet minister has ever attended an international joint commission public meeting, we feel it to be very essential that a committee be formed comprising members of parliament-not engineers-to meet with members of this association and discuss the problems of the property owners, and consider the most economical ways of protecting their homes and income. Considering the enormous losses already sustained, they wish to be assured of a reasonably safe future.
We feel that had the international joint commission recommended the hydro commission to lower the channels two feet, the power potentials, and the natural levels of the lake would have been maintained, and erosion controlled without further protection.
We feel that this matter should be considered immediately, a committee formed, and action taken so that protective work may be completed in conjunction with the completion of the St. Lawrence power project.
I might say also in that connection that I have a letter from the Wentworth county council endorsing that brief. I wish to draw your attention especially to the second last paragraph of that brief, which states:
We feel that had the international joint commission recommended the hydro commission to lower the channels two feet, the power potentials, and the natural levels of the lake would have been maintained, and erosion controlled without further protection.
I must say that this brief was presented by an association that represents other smaller associations from the bay of Quinte around the lake to Niagara-on-the-Lake. In connection with the recent damage I wish to say that I have before me a list of 139 different properties along the shores of lake Ontario. I might say it refers to just that part of lake Ontario extending from Burlington to Niagara-on-the-Lake. The totals of that list are as follows:	Estimated damage,
$361,034.20; real estate depreciation, $415,095, and cost of protection by shoring, etc., $365,709.25. Just last year in one storm alone damage was done to the total amount of $12,180 to 24 dwellings at Crescent beach, Saltfleet township, near Hamilton.
It is often said, Mr. Speaker, that the federal authorities have no responsibility in the matter. I say they most certainly have because, so far as lake shore erosion is concerned, in the past many years federal governments have taken tons of sand from along the lake several miles from shore, making huge holes in the lake bottom. These holes were very quickly refilled by sand washed from the shores by the undertow, and that sand never returned to the lake shore.
These people on the shores on lake Ontario who have their property damaged are not

asking for any consideration for the damage that has been done, but they are concerned for the future and they want to be assured that they will have adequate protection with respect to damage that might occur through the operations of the deep sea waterway. On January 23, 1956, I wrote to General McNaughton, chairman of the Canadian section of the international joint commission, as follows:
Dear General McNaughton;
I would urge that in the forthcoming deliberations that there be suitable indemnification clauses inserted into the plan for the regulations of the water levels of lake Ontario. I urge this on behalf of the lake Ontario property protection association and more especially for those members and residents who live on that portion of the shores of lake Ontario lying between Hamilton and Niagara-on-the-Lake.
On the same date I received this letter from General McNaughton:
Dear Mr. Lennard:
I have your letter of today's date in which you urge on behalf of the lake Ontario property protection association and others that the plan for the regulation of the levels of lake Ontario should include suitable indemnification clauses. I am bringing your letter to the attention of my colleagues and careful consideration will be given to the matter.
Yours sincerely,
A. G. L. McNaughton.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, these people are very fair. They are not asking for compensation for past losses, but they are asking for protection against future damage. I feel that in this whole affair the property owners along the shores of lake Ontario have had to play second fiddle to the Ontario HydroElectric Power Commission, and that under the circumstances they should be assured of protection in the future. Protection clauses most certainly should be put into the agreement.
