speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the resolution moved by my colleague the hon. member for Kootenay West, I wish to co-operate, as have other members, by being as brief as possible because we know there are so many who would like to make their contribution to the debate. The resolution calls for a dominion-provincial conference to study the question of conservation with respect to soil, forest and water resources. In introducing the resolution the hon. member has set out most adequately and in excellent fashion what the objectives are and some of the means that might be pursued. Therefore I will not need to repeat what has been said in the general discussion of the question.
However, the province of Manitoba is particularly interested from the point of view of

water. So far this winter more than seven feet of snow have fallen in most parts of the province, and unless the spring break-up is exceptionally favourable there is no doubt at all that there will be widespread property losses as well as inestimable damage to soil and fields generally. Because we in Manitoba feel that in the past there has not been sufficient planning with respect to the conservation of water, which is the other aspect of the problem of flooding, we are particularly glad that this question has come before the house at this time.
So far the only type of work that has been done which could be classed as conservation, together with reclamation, has been that done under the authority of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and most people in Manitoba feel that while the act has been very useful in many respects it has been too restricted in its scope, not only from the point of view that it applies only to the three prairie provinces but also because it does not even apply to all of the three prairie provinces.
For example, in the province of Manitoba the work done under the act has been confined to a small area in the southwestern part of the province. There are large settled areas of good agricultural land where the problem of flood waters has been just as serious as in the area covered by the act, if not more so, and these areas have been entirely left out of the operation of the act. The figures show what the situation has been. Since the act came into force on April 1, 1935 until March 31 last year over $100 million has been spent. Of that amount only $6,824,000 was spent in the province of Manitoba. About $45 million was spent in Saskatchewan, the same amount in Alberta and $3,242,000 in British Columbia. Percentagewise it works out to 6-8 per cent in Manitoba, 45 per cent in Alberta, the same in Saskatchewan and 3-2 per cent in British Columbia.
I point that out not because we have any objection to a large amount of money being spent for conservation and reclamation in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. We are glad they have been able to receive benefits under the act, but certainly even a glance at the figures will indicate that we in the province of Manitoba have a real grievance in that only 6-8 per cent of the total has been spent in our province where the need, particularly for flood control, is as great as if not greater than in the other provinces. For that reason I welcome the proposal for a dominion-provincial conference on the question of conservation, particularly from the point of view of the question of water in the province of Manitoba.
Conservation
We are interested in the matter from two different angles, which stem from the same condition. We are interested in flood control for the very obvious reason that in the last three or four years many parts of the province, such as the interlake district represented by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), the constituency which I represent and many other areas have suffered very serious set-backs due to excess water, and also due to the fact that the run-off of water was not controlled.
We are also interested because while our province so far has been extremely fortunate in being able to utilize its water power, we are now reaching the stage where the easily accessible sources of water power are becoming exhausted. Unless we move much farther north into areas which are much more inaccessible and remote, a procedure which would bring with it much greater expenditure on transmission facilities and construction, it will not be long before the province of Manitoba will become extremely short of water power. If we can harness in the most useful fashion the water resources we have and can control the water run-off, it will serve a double purpose. It will provide a supply of water for our water power requirements and at the same time it will prevent some of the serious flood damage that has occurred in our province from time to time.
In order to bring about a general over-all plan for the control of these waters, it will be necessary to have federal and provincial co-operation. In the province of Manitoba I think there is a good case in point. As it happens, in the northwest part of Manitoba, the area with which I am most familiar, the difficulties we have had with flood water arise from two sources particularly. One of them happens to be Riding Mountain national park, which is the responsibility of the federal government. The other one, which is north of Riding Mountain national park, is the Duck Mountain reserve which is, of course, the responsibility of the province of Manitoba. The waters from the eastern and northern slopes of these two watersheds have caused a serious amount of damage over the years, and many efforts have been made by the municipalities, through the province, to obtain the co-operation of the federal government in working out an over-all plan to try to control the water from these watersheds in such a way that the problem will be solved.
The problem in the past has been this. While the federal government has been willing to assist and has contributed to a great number of projects, the assistance has been based or hypothecated upon the ability of the local municipality to contribute its

Conservation
share. They have offered to the province a series of agreements under which the rural municipality and the province share half the cost of construction of the project, and the federal government assumes the other half. But unless the local municipality can put up its share, then of course all the rest of the moneys which are contingent upon that share being forthcoming do not come through.
We have therefore been slowly coming to the realization that if we are going to solve our flooding problem in that part of the province-and I think this statement holds true for many other parts of my province- that job must be done. It will be a big scale job. It will require excellent engineering and large expenditures, but it will pay big dividends, when we stop to consider what is lost in the way of crops and soil erosion each spring when the waters go out of control, as has happened so many times in the last few years.
It has happened in the constituency which I represent. It has happened on the Portage plains, in the interlake country and in many other parts of Manitoba. The loss in topsoil, in crops and in property damage has been tremendous in my province.
While this is of course a long-term project and it may take a considerable length of time to work out a national policy of conservation, in the meantime I hope this government will be willing, in co-operation with the province of Manitoba, to take some immediate steps to help reduce the losses which we may be facing even this spring on account of the unusually heavy snowfall.

Mr. Speaker, I am nappy to take part in this debate which I consider very important to the future welfare of the electors of the county I have the honour to represent in this house, and of all Canadians as well.
It is not the first time I call the attention of this house on this question, but I think it is such an important matter that I never miss an opportunity to speak on the subject.
Since Providence has been good enough to endow our country with all kinds of resources, our duty is to develop, protect and improve these resources. Our deserving Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) having been good enough to give us such a brilliant and active Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage), it is our
[Mr. Zaplitny.I
duty to support him and to acquaint him with our wishes.
For my part, I wish that the Nation river project, which was prepared several years ago, would be undertaken. I have a plan which is already drawn up, and I would be glad to submit a copy of that plan to the house, to the minister. I will read the different parts I would like to put on the official record.
(Text):
Chapter 1
Location and Boundaries
The watershed of the South Nation river is an area of 1,511 square miles lying between the cities of Ottawa and Hawkesbury on the river Ottawa and Brockville on the river St. Lawrence. In shape it may be likened to a flattened triangle with its apex near Gloucester station, six miles south of Ottawa and the long side, or base, running northeast from near Brockville to a point near Vankleek Hill, Southwest of Hawkesbury. On the southeast and for a short distance on the southwest the South Nation watershed is bounded by that of the St. Lawrence. On the north, it adjoins the watershed of the Ottawa and on the west the watershed of the Rideau, whose tributary, Kemptville creek rises within ten miles of the St. Lawrence, north of Brockville.
A watershed has been defined as the high ground separating two river systems. Taken in this literal sense it becomes only a boundary line but the term "watershed" is commonly used also to describe the area which is drained by a river and its tributaries. It is in this broader sense that the term is used in this report and, throughout the report, the terms watershed, drainage area, drainage basin and drainage unit are used interchangeably.
As there are no doubt many others who will want to speak on this important subject, I shall leave off further discussion of this important chapter 1. I will ask that this important subject be given consideration and that everything possible be done for the conservation of the soil and the power resources. I should like to have the minister, when he has the opportunity to do so, to look into the matter.
(Translation) :
As I said just now in English, the watershed of the southern branch of the Nation river covers an area of 1,511 square miles.
There are neither cities nor towns of any importance in this watershed, but a number of fine, prosperous villages that have been incorporated as municipalities, among them Winchester, Chesterville, Casselman, Finch and Maxville. There are also several villages that have not been incorporated as municipalities, of which Spencerville, South Mountain, Chrysler, Metcalfe, Moose Creek, Limoges, Russell and Bourget, are the most important.

We can therefore see that this watershed really comprises a rural area in Ontario.
I am speaking of digging, diking, etc., all urgent and necessary works, because they would improve the position of the twelve municipalities: Matilda, Mounta, Winchester, Edwardsburg, Augusta, Finch, Cambridge, Plantagenet South, Alfred, Plantagenet North, Chesterville and Casselman.
Floods in the southern watershed of the Nation river constitute a serious threat to the very existence of the people of all the rural municipalities in that district, and are detrimental to the economy of all the neighbouring commercial centres. It goes without saying that the periodical destruction of crops, roads, bridges and the washing away of thousands of tons of the best arable soil in one section of the province constitute a loss for the whole province. Those large losses are unfortunately not rare occurrences; on the contrary, they have been felt 30 times in the past 37 years, from 1918 to 1955 inclusive and in six cases they happened twice during the same year.
The floods of 1938 and 1955, which were the worst of all, indicate that this menace is getting worse and worse all the time.
The worst floods happen more particularly in two districts, the Brinston area, up the river from Chesterville which comprises the fertile lands of Winchester, Matilda and Mountain townships and the lake Cobb area, including the lowlands along the river from Lemieux to Plantagenet. In the Brinston district, the 1938 flood covered an area of 24 square miles; the water rose as high as nine feet and many houses had from two to three feet of water on the ground floor. The 1947 flood was quite as serious.
Floods caused by swelling rivers in the Spring cause much trouble, havoc and distress. Farmers are doing all they can to face the threat; they put livestock and equipment in attics or other safe shelters, and put off seeding until the water has withdrawn. At times, as many as nine days and a half have elapsed between the time the river overflowed its banks and Anally receded.
Those floods happen not only during the spring thaws but often in summer after heavy rains. As a matter of fact those rains cause the heaviest damage, for at such times full crops are washed away or rot under the water. Cases have been reported where the same farmer had his crops destroyed four years in a row.
I am glad that the minister concerned has agreed to accept a copy of the report, and I
Conservation
assure him that I am prepared at all times to supply him with any information regarding that project.
The cost of the project is not particularly high, being somewhat over two million dollars, to be shared by the province and the federal government. Since this work would be carried out in an agricultural district the municipalities concerned are in no position to meet any part of the cost. However, irrigation works are being carried out everywhere in Canada, the cost being met partly by the federal government, partly by the provincial governments. In the case of the project I just mentioned, the flooding of thousands of acres of fertile land could be prevented. Moreover we would be able to restock the Nation river with fish such as those our forebears caught and which they so enjoyed talking about. I will return to this later, and I shall refer to the three dams which existed in former days and which belonged to private individuals who had built sawmills and flour mills on them. Those mills later disappeared because of a lack of forest cover, of neglect and lack of funds.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, if this project of mine were carried out, the river would stretch over 90 miles that could easily be stocked with various kinds of fish, to the delight of tourists and residents of the twelve municipalities I have mentioned. Moreover, this would also provide a supply of drinking water for all the herds on the numerous riverside farms, as about thirty small streams, such as the smaller and greater Castor rivers, the Horse creek and several others, flow into the Nation river. These rivers, which run through several villages, would provide a reservoir of a fairly high level that would insure adequate year round protection against fire.
You might be surprised to learn that, last summer my home town of Casselman voted $25,000 for the construction of a dam across the Nation river, to raise the level of the water in order to pump it back more readily into mains, to insure protection against fire.
That would enable us to have irrigation ditches in different parts and in many cases to double the crops of our farmers. It is not only in the west that irrigation would be a good thing. We too in the east, in the province of Ontario, would like to have irrigation just as much as the western provinces. However I do not want to impose upon the kindness of the house and have it listen to speeches on that subject for days and weeks. I realize that the government, which manages our country so well, will always be prepared to undertake projects

Conservation
which are to the benefit of all Canadians and will try to solve that problem when it has enough revenue to do so.
But I want to call the attention of the house on that point and say that in the east we maintain that the government should undertake an irrigation scheme in order to help our farmers who have to buy from the west most of the grain they need to feed their cattle. Yes, Mr. Speaker, our farmers and the people of our villages have to spend thousands and thousands of dollars in order to get water.
I know farmers in my county who spent more than $2,000 to provide their cattle with an adequate supply of water. The same farmers buy grain from the west at market price, and very often pay $20 a ton for transportation only, in addition to storage fees. They sell their products at market price, as the western farmers do, but they do not come here and ask parliament to guarantee bank loans on their farm stored crops, nor to vote a $65 million bonus as the one we gave a few years ago to the western farmers. But they work just the same 365 days a year and they know that the province of Ontario contributes' 45 per cent of the federal budget. I trust that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will take my request into serious consideration.
There is also the Ottawa river which, on a distance of 40 miles approximately, borders on the northern part of the county of Russell, that is from Rockcliffe to Wendover. I shall limit my remarks to the part of that river which flows through the county of Russell. Cottage and motel owners are getting discouraged because they are losing customers owing to the pollution of the Ottawa river water by sewage and waste material from Ottawa and other cities, and from industries.
I believe the provinces of Ontario and Quebec should join the federal government in an attempt to solve the problem of purification and restocking of the Ottawa river. The fish have been destroyed by polluted water. This keeps away the tourists and means a loss to all cottage owners, as their properties decrease in value.
I would chide myself if I failed to mention the urgent need of accelerating reforestation work. May I be permitted to relate what Russell county has done in this field. We began retimbering 28 years ago in what we call the Larose stand. Now I know that the federal government is anxious to provide all the help needed without however encroaching upon provincial rights. Therefore the minis-

ter should try and get the Ontario government more interested. The Larose forest entails rather heavy expenses for the united counties of Prescott and Russell who buy land and pay wages to an officer, while the province is taking care of it as far as planting and maintenance are concerned.
I am pleased to congratulate all the personnel working on that project. They are wonderful workers and our agronomist is an efficient and intelligent man. They are doing a very good job. I give credit to the provincial government in this respect. This forest is a provincial property, so that the counties have to pay for the lands, and municipalities are losing tax revenue.
However, we are satisfied to carry on, because it will profit the future generation. At present, the Larose forest has an area of 23,500 acres, planted with 12 million trees. We mean to increase it to 25 million trees, that is why I am urging federal government assistance.
I have been interested in reforestation for the past 40 years. I started to plant trees on my farms in 1931, and I have had over 250,000 trees planted. What discourages people who want to do the same thing is the fact that at present the Ontario government is selling trees for $10 to $14 per thousand. In addition, one must pay municipal taxes and fire insurance. If the provincial government refuses to supply trees free of charge, could not the federal government pay for them? I would also ask that taxes be payable only when the trees are cut, and that the services of provincial government experts be provided to tell us which trees should be planted. I would also ask that fire insurance premiums be reasonably priced so that farmers may be encouraged to retimber all those stretches of land unsuited to agriculture. And we have a great many left. There are a great many of these stretches in Russell. It would be far better if they were covered with trees. In this way we would be providing wealth for future generations.
While travelling through Europe, a few years ago, I made it a point to inquire about methods of reforestation in the various countries I visited. The method I have just described was explained to me. I should add that when a tree is to be cut an expert from the central government designates the particular tree to be felled, and at the same time orders its immediate replacement by a small tree or trees suited to the ground. Then, and then only does the owner pay taxes and fire insurance premiums.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that afforestation is essential to the economy

of Canada and that the sooner we set ourselves to this task the better it will be for all Canadians. I am pleased to tell the house -in fact, both the opposition side and the government side of the house share this opinion-that the prime minister's choice was perfect when he picked so active and so qualified a man as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to direct the work of that department. All Canada will benefit from his great capacity.
Mr. Speaker, it is important to hasten the carrying out of this project. I therefore hope that the provinces will better understand their duty in that respect and that, in the near future, afforestation will be practised on a larger scale. This will also bring about an increase of animal life and attract greater numbers of American tourists who live close to our border.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution in the name of the hon. member for Kootenay West calls for the establishment of a nation-wide policy on soil, forest and water conservation and land use for Canada. I feel that most of us thoroughly agree in principle at least with the hon. member's resolution.
Therefore let us first make an observation on soil. I think many of us have oftentimes picked up a lump of soil in our hands, and we who are farmers have sifted that soil through our fingers and felt its body, its texture and its availability to absorb water. Yes, a farmer will sniff at it and almost taste it.
No treasure on earth is as valuable as a simple lump of soil. It is the very core of life from which all organisms emerge and it is the basis of the prosperity of all nations. A lump of soil absorbs water and solar energy and harbours a swarm of living things. A tiny seed finds in it the heat and moisture necessary to germinate. Here too is a storehouse of food from which tiny rootlets derive nourishment that is passed along to stems, leaves and fruit; all this from a single lump of soil. However, the soil can only give forth what it possesses. If rich in nutritive elements it can produce an abundance of food for man or beast. Lacking such reserves it can only grow weak plants and poor crops.
Originally nature had provided in the arable lands the nutriment required to grow a good crop, but man through lack of foresight to conserve depleted nature's storehouse, slowly in some parts of the world, in others very rapidly. Where soils have been depleted in organic material through mismanagement
Conservation
or other contributing conditions, science has intervened. It has provided improved methods of tillage. With chemical fertilizers it adds to the soil required quantities of the food it lacks. It has even developed custom-made seeds, brimfull of strength and vitality which enclose all the desirable characteristics of species, variety, productivity, early maturing, rapidity of growth and resistance to disease.
How important is a tree? The answer to this question is wide and varied. I would just like to quote an article that was written at the beginning of the 18th century, as follows:
The state is like a tree, the roots are agriculture, the trunk is the population, the branches are industry, the leaves are commerce and the arts; it is from the roots that the tree draws the nourishing sap . . . and it is to the roots that a remedy must be applied if the tree is not to perish.
In conservation in Canada the federal government should be giving direction and leadership to the production and growing of that tree so it will be worthy of being conserved. The roots of the tree are our provincial governments, which over the years have spent many thousands of dollars promoting conservation at the provincial level. The trunk and branches could be the population and industry, who stand to benefit from a sound tree with firm roots.
Governments in the past and present show great interest in our natural resources, but are they too late? They become concerned not in the relatively simple matter of protecting, developing and using the resources, but with the costly and almost hopeless task of restoring, rebuilding or trying to recreate or re-establish something that was in perfect condition before they became interested.
Conservation of our resources, including our soil, forests and water, should be a challenge for our governments at all levels. It should be a challenge to every individual in this great country of ours. I believe it is time for all of us to accept this challenge to prevent the waste of those things that represent our very lifeblood.
At the time of the birth of Christ it has been estimated that there were presumably about 300 million people on earth. Since then the population has doubled on three successive occasions. It took 1,650 years for the first doubling; 200 years for the second doubling, and only 100 years for the most recent. By the end of this century, barring unforeseen casualties, the world population will have again doubled. Should the population reach the 5 billion mark by the end of the century there will then be only an average of half an acre of ground per person. If

Conservation
these facts were really understood there would be no need for us to talk about and urge the necessity for conservation; we would be hard at it.
The virgin forest lands of this continent have been sadly depleted. In many areas we lose to fire, insects, disease and harvesting an amount in excess of the total annual growth. Forest management to maintain a sustained yield is still an objective to be achieved. In Canada an average of 5,000 fires a year rage across our forest lands burning in their path enough timber to build 85,000 five-room houses.
Forest fire protection in the Scandinavian country of Sweden is so complete that it is cheaper to insure a woodland property than it is to insure an industrial concern. To us living in Canada, where no insurance company would give consideration to covering growing timber, this fact is little short of incredible.
The demand for our forest products is terrific. For example, a single Sunday edition of the New York Times uses the product of from 80 to 100 acres of forest. I think we should also remember that it takes 60 to 80 years to grow a black spruce to a size ready for economical pulpwood harvesting.
I should like to conclude by quoting an poem entitled "Dust Bowl" which appeared in Nature Magazine of December, 1954. I hope that we in Canada will never reach the condition described here. This reads:
Men now exhume dead roads from tragic dust, That devastation's dry wind-blowings spanned, Where nature's grim revenge rides every gust,
For man's abuse of its long-tortured land.
Too late, bulldozers seek to rectify
The checks and balances where man has erred,
Too late, steam shovels fret dust-heavy sky,
For nature-it seems-has the final word.
Now man must face destruction, he designed, While lord-of-all-creation's worthy foe,
Will blow soil-desiccation through his mind, Exacting punishment with every blow.
A noble servant-nature-but beware,
Contempt will draw a monster from its lair.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been wondering all this evening whether I was going to get on. Possibly that may have been the result of something affecting Mr. Speaker. Possibly I should call in an eye specialist. Since the last speaker was not an hon. member on this side of the house I thought possibly I might follow. Perhaps I should blame my mother for this, because apparently she did not make me quite big enough or tall enough.
First I should like to congratulate the hon. members who have preceded me in this debate upon their sincere presentations in the cause of conservation. It is evident that more and more people are today conscious of the need [Mr. McBain.l
for conserving our natural resources. The majority of hon. members who have taken part in this debate have dealt with conservation as it affects their ridings, with the exception of one, the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais). He, in my opinion, is a national conservationist. He included everything in his amendment with one exception, the wildlife resources, which to me and the people in my country are very important. If I wished to amend the amendment I would include wildlife, but I do not think I shall move any subamendment at this time.
The question of conservation is tied up with the privilege of living in Canada. Durward Allen said in his book "Our Wild Life Legacy":
The rich resources of this land have given us our national standing and character, but we have reached a point where an end to much of this common property is in sight. The question is whether we will use it wisely and in perpetuity or use it up and be done with it. It is clear that natural advantage lies in one course although as individuals we might profit by the other.
Other speakers in this debate have covered the many and varied subjects of conservation, such as forestry, mining, soil erosion, agriculture, water, etc. I should like to deal with some aspects of the subject in regard to forests and wildlife, two of our renewable resources.
We are aware that during the early years in both the United States and Canada our forests were greatly depleted and our wildlife was killed off with no regard for future generations. In recent years it has become evident that if we are to continue to supply the demand for our forest products, a more efficient utilization of our forests is necessary. The federal government has been aware of the need for co-operation with the provinces in this field, and as a result the forestry act of 1949 was passed. This act provides for assistance to the provinces in the fields of forest inventories, reforestation, infestation of forests, etc. In this year's estimates you will find that $900,000 is being contributed for forest inventories. An additional $225,000 is being contributed for reforestation. There is also an amount of $650,000, which represents the federal contribution to combat spruce budworm in the province of New Brunswick.
Under the forestry branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources a great deal has been done in the field of forest research. It has also carried on research in forest products in the Vancouver and Ottawa laboratories. The maintenance of the operations of this important branch of government will cost $2J million this year. These figures, along with the contributions I have mentioned, total in

the neighbourhood of $4| million. It is quite obvious, therefore, that this government is aware of the need for forest conservation and is playing its part. I might add that responsibilities in the field of conservation should not be borne only by governments alone but also by the lumber industry and those individuals who derive pleasure and recreation from the great forests of Canada.
I should like to deal briefly with the subject of forest conservation as it affects the Northwest Territories. For a number of years the Slave river has produced spruce lumber for our building requirements and the logging and timber requirements of our mining industry, but it has reached the point where in two years the supply along this river will have been exhausted. The natural resources of the Northwest Territories are a federal responsibility, and I would respectfully suggest to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources that an immediate survey be carried out by the forestry branch of his department to ascertain whether natural reforestation in that area is possible and if not, what methods of reforestation would be necessary to assure the ever-increasing mining industry and the communities of the north of a continued supply of these forest products.
I should also like to point out to the minister the need for a sound forest management policy in view of the new lumber industry which has been set up in the Wood Buffalo park.
Now I should like to make a few brief remarks in regard to the conservation of wildlife. We have only to look back not too many years when hundreds of thousands of buffalo roamed the western plains. In the matter of a few short years after the building of the railroads to the west, the buffalo were on the verge of extinction. A lessening in the numbers of these animals was bound to come because the people of that era gave no heed to conservation, and their disappearance was sudden. Many hardships were encountered by the people living in the west at that time. Through government action since that time we have been sustaining herds of buffalo in some of our national parks, one of which is the Wood Buffalo park, which lies partly in my riding. The herd in this area has increased from approximately 650 animals in 1890 to between 15,000 and 16,000 at the present time.
Another example of what could happen when conservation is thrown to the winds is the case of the whooping crane. Today in North America it is believed there are only 27 of these birds left. I am happy to say that the majority of these birds nest in my
Conservation
constituency in the Northwest Territories. Because of regulations in both the United States and Canada forbidding the shooting of these whooping cranes it is hoped that in the future their numbers will increase.
From the sentimental and recreational point of view we in Canada through our national parks and provincial game preserves, along with projects carried on by private organizations and individuals such as Ducks Unlimited and the Jack Miner bird sanctuary, are attempting to preserve some our our truly Canadian species of wildlife. I would like at this time to commend these private organizations for the active part they are playing in the conservation program, both in the United States and Canada.
Nineteen federal-provincial conferences have been held since 1922 on the subject of wildlife conservation. I understand that the twentieth meeting will take place some time in June of this year. I do not intend to go fully into the matter of the part played by the government in the conservation of wildlife, but I should like to say that the wildlife conservation branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is co-operating fully with provincial and private agencies in the broad aspects of wildlife research and management.
An example of this co-operation is the case of migratory game birds. The Canadian wildlife service, along with the United States fish and wildlife service, some provincial governments, Ducks Unlimited and other private organizations, conducts surveys each year to determine the current status of our migratory birds, particularly ducks and geese. Joint reports are prepared annually which provide information upon which to base regulations governing their shooting. Many other surveys of other species of wildlife are made throughout Canada by this branch and the results of these surveys are made available to provincial governments and other interested parties.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak more specifically of conservation as it affects the Northwest Territories. To me conservation is the intelligent use of our natural resources in the Northwest Territories, and in that part of the country conservation is also an economic problem. A large section of our population, and I speak of the Indians and Eskimos particularly, derive their living from the trapping of fur-bearing animals, and they also derive a large portion of their food from our wildlife resources.
In order to give an idea of what has happened to the trapping industry during recent years I should like to quote a few figures. In 1943-44 the total number of beaver pelts

Conservation
exported from the Northwest Territories was 13,535. In 1954-55 the figure was 11,342. The total value in 1943-44 was $463,574. The total value in 1954-55 was $168,996. Then let us take the case of ermine. I doubt very much if there are very many here who know what ermine is. There are a few from the northern part of the country who know, but some of our city slickers would not know the difference between an ermine and a rabbit. As far as ermine or weasel-now you all know-is concerned, in 1943-44 9,790 ermine were taken and exported. In 1954-55 4,852 were exported. The value in 1943-44 was $13,706. Last year the value was $4,124.
Then we come to mink. In 1943-44 the total export was 9,903 skins. In 1954-55 the figure was 3,463 skins, one-third of the number taken in 1943-44. Some people will say, and I have heard this argument before, that the number of furs taken is dependent on the price paid. Well, as I have just said, in 1943-44 some 9,903 mink were taken and the value at that time was $21.25 each. Last year when 3,463 were taken the value was $23.10 each, practically the same.
What has happened? The numbers of furbearing animals in my part of the country are being depleted. We will go on to muskrat, the main source of livelihood for my people down the Mackenzie river. In 1943-44 there were 281,255 muskrats taken. In 1948-49 there were 724,432 taken. Last year there were 344,507. Let me deal with the difference in revenue between 1943 and last year with respect to rats, and I am not referring to the rats that a member of the C.C.F. party spoke about the other day. I am talking about muskrats. The value in 1943-44 was $528,759 compared with $248,090 last year.
Then let us take white fox. For as long as I can remember white fox has been the commodity from which the Eskimo has derived his cash. In 1943-44 there were 30,420 white fox skins exported. Last year 6,877 white fox were exported. To me these figures indicate an alarming decrease not only in the number of furs taken but in the revenue to the people of my part of the country.
I will leave fur for one minute. Economically speaking, fur is that industry which supplies the native with cash in order to buy the white man's food to which he has become accustomed over the years. But now I will speak of caribou. Caribou is and has been the main source of food for the native people. I should like to refer to a survey made by Dr. Banfield of the Canadian wildlife service in 1948. In that survey Dr. Ban-field estimated that the total population of caribou at that time was 658,000. He also
[Mr. Hardie.l
estimated the total decrease per year taking into consideration on the one hand the calf crop and on the other hand the decrease brought about by hunting, what the wolves take, natural disease and so on. At that time he said our caribou population was decreasing by 50,000 animals a year.
I and a lot of other people in my constituency said, "That guy is nuts." As a matter of fact, this is a controversial subject in my constituency. There are a great number of people in my constituency who say these experts are completely off their rockers. There are other people in my constituency who agree with the experts. Now, I am a layman.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: I do not know whom I should listen to, whether I should listen to the people in my constituency who say that the experts are crazy or whether I should listen to the experts. But I will say one thing. Last year the same department, namely the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, through its Canadian wildlife service undertook a survey of caribou. What did they find?

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Caribou.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: My dear friend, I am sorry to say they did not find caribou in the numbers in which they expected to find them. What did they find?

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Muskrat.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) does not know anything else but wheat. If he will just shut his trap I will continue.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lethbridge did not say a word.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: If the hon. member for Lethbridge did not say anything I am very sorry for the remark I made, and I will withdraw it. It must have been another wheat farmer from Alberta.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Was it the hon. member for Cariboo?

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
What happened? They came out, and as a result of their surveys last year they said the caribou population had been depleted to from 300,000 to 350,000 animals, thus leaving us in the north and your Eskimo and Indian friends 300,000 caribou as of last spring. Dr. Banfield's report, which we said was crazy-I said it; I agreed with many people-stated that the caribou were diminishing or were being depleted by 50,000 animals a year. After last year's survey-50,000 a year for six years,

300,000-we find that is practically what they are missing now. We now have 300,000 caribou left in the Northwest Territories.
To my friends on all sides of this house this may seem to be nothing. They started feeding the natives beefsteak. I want to tell my hon. friends something. This case is not the same as that of the buffalo. When the buffalo disappeared from the western plains the prairie farmer brought in livestock that could live off the same grazing grounds as those on which the buffalo had been feeding. I will defy the Minister of Agriculture or anybody else to feed cattle on the same grazing grounds the caribou have been feeding on this last century.
This is an important matter. I am appealing to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to do something about it. I know what people will say. As a matter of fact, I have heard officials of the department say it. They will say that we have at Tuktoyaktuk a reindeer herd that the government brought in 30 years ago. We spent over $1 million on those reindeer. By the time they arrived at Tuktoyaktuk there were 3,600 of them. Twenty or more years later, how many reindeer have we at Tuktoyaktuk? We have 6,500.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Plus Rudolph.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I will tell you this. Of all hon. members to speak of Rudolph, I think the hon. member has the reddest nose. As I was saying, we have spent over $1 million on reindeer. We have not quite doubled the numbers of those reindeer in over 20 years. I must admit that we have supplied meat to some of the people up there at anything from 65 to 75 cents a pound. We might as well have been flying in beef.
Then down in Wood Buffalo park we have the buffalo which I mentioned some time ago. We have increased the population from 650 in 1890 to from 15,000 to 16,000 today. We have also slaughtered each year a certain number of those buffalo and we have sold them to the Hudson's Bay Company, who sold them back to us. That is fine and dandy; it is O.K. with me. But last year what did they do? I am not a farmer, so 1 thought I would bring up this matter in the estimates committee last year. They sold buffalo meat to Canada Packers and to Burns and Company for 5 cents a pound, f.o.b. Fort Smith. But the same department sold the same buffalo meat to the Department of Indian Affairs for 35 cents a pound for distribution as relief rations to the Indians. When I brought this matter before the estimates committee last year I thought the hon. member for Moose
Conservation
Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher), a real cattleman, would be sure to nab this point, but he just let it go by.
To be serious about this matter, Mr. Speaker, may I say that something must be done. At the rate caribou have been depleting in numbers, six years from now there will not be one living caribou in the Northwest Territories. This is the food of the large majority of the people who live in that country. To the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources I suggest that he really get down on his knees before the Minister of Finance-

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: That I must see.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Now who has the red nose?

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
-and do something during this period about restricting the number of caribou that are taken each year. If the natives do not take those caribou-and of course if we are to follow sound conservation policies we shall be obliged to restrict the number of caribou they take-something must be done to feed these people. But when I look at the estimates this year I find they are less than they were last year. That may be all right, but I have not found that there has been any increase to provide these people with meat. Something must be done, Mr. Speaker.
Now I shall leave buffalo for a minute and come back to the reindeer situation. We brought in these reindeer, and the idea was that we would do so in order to provide the starving people with meat. After we brought in the reindeer the government decided that it would be a fine idea to distribute these reindeer to certain Eskimo families who would herd them and live off them. At the slaughtering season, in August or September, when these reindeer were fat they would move them in to the reindeer station and slaughter them and sell the meat to the Eskimos, the Hudson's Bay Company or any other white people. That was fine. It sounded good. As a matter of fact I think I even heard in the estimates committee talk about extending this idea to other parts of the country, putting more reindeer in other parts of the Northwest Territories. Well, herding reindeer is not the same as ranching cattle. In so far as cattle are concerned, you put up a fence and the cattle stay inside. The reindeer are roving over 549,000 square miles of country.
These Eskimos are the sort of people, like you and me, who like to visit with their friends once in a while. Put yourselves in their position. They follow a herd of these reindeer around the country. They say the

Conservation
reindeer is okay and they eat it, but once in a while they like to see something other than reindeer. They say to themselves, let us go and visit Joe Kuhali, 100 miles away. It is Easter time, and that is a good time to go away. They go away and leave the reindeer. When they come back where are the reindeer? They start running around and finally get half of them back, but half of them are gone. Do you know where they have gone? The caribou move through the country in a wild state during the migration period, and the reindeer follow suit. Reindeer have been shot at Muskox lake, 1,500 miles away from the reindeer station.
As a matter of fact I had a trapper say to me, "A funny thing, I shot a caribou yesterday and this caribou had half its ear cut off; I never saw that before." He said it was cut; there was no fooling about it. Sometimes at the reindeer station they cut half an ear to mark a certain animal for a certain band in which they put him. This reminds me of a story about the difference between caribou and reindeer. A few years back there was an Indian, I think his name was Joe Blondin, who was up around Fort Normandin and Aklavik, and he shot what he thought was a caribou. What happened? The police brought him in because he had shot a reindeer, not a caribou.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: It was not Tucker?

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: You had better not go up there.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
You took the words right out of my mouth, my friend. What happened? They brought this man in and charged him with shooting a reindeer, a protected animal. Of course they held court and the crown prosecutor was there. The Indian defended himself. The crown prosecutor said, "Now, there must be some difference between a reindeer and a caribou." Of course he did not know. They called in a scientist. The scientist said that so far as he was aware the only difference between a caribou and a reindeer-I do not know which way it was- was that the caribou's tooth was so many millimeters longer than the reindeer or vice versa. In any event, this man was expected to go out into the wild, open up this animal's jaw and measure the teeth. However, it happened we had a very fair magistrate at that time and this man was set free.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I would say to this house that caribou mean no more to the average person in Canada, and I could talk until I am blue in the face, than the buffalo

did before the railroads went west. But in my part of the country they are the very lifeblood. We eat this animal. Something has to be done. I am not a scientist, and I do not know the difference between a tooth of one animal and another. I cannot give you the answers but I am sure the department of northern affairs, through its Canadian wildlife service, knows the answer. I am hoping that the Northwest Territories administration, which also comes under that department, will do something about the recommendations and the results of the surveys that have been conducted by the Canadian wildlife service.
I should also like to say that we are trying to educate our people in that part of the country in conservation measures. There is one book I would suggest should be a part of that curriculum, a book written by Deward Allen entitled "Our Wild Life Legacy". It should be not only in the grade schools of that country but also in the high schools. It should be put into the trapper's associations, because this book will tell those people more about conservation that I could ever tell them.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote a paragraph I once read. I do not know the name of the author, but perhaps someone may know who he is after I have read it. He is the person who should be credited with it. He says:
Because man has made hash of nature's system of checks and balances, he finds he must go to a lot of trouble from time to time to straighten out his mishandling of the resources given him by nature. But he seems to go about it the hard way, making the same mistakes and trying the same remedies again and again. He plunders the resources, then works overtime to restore them or find a substitute.
I hope that the federal government, who are responsible for the wildlife resources of the Northwest Territories, will have learned from the experience of the United States and all the other provinces of Canada, and will not make the same mistakes over again.
I wish to adjourn the debate.
